competency_fulfillment.rationale: Every item lays out three tiled cases before asking 'Which rule always gives the number of tiles?', so the learner generalizes from evidence instead of recalling a stated formula, which is what inductive derivation means. The evidence actually forces the keyed rule in each item: in seed 605 the case 'a 5 by 2 rectangle takes 10 tiles' is equally matched by doubling the length, but 'a 7 by 5 rectangle takes 35 tiles' kills that reading, and in seed 501 'a 4 by 4 square takes 16 tiles' is equally matched by four times the side until 'a 5 by 5 square takes 25 tiles' rules it out. Checking all 14 samples, exactly one offered option survives all three cases in every item.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Both figures the competency names are covered: eight rectangle items keyed to 'length × width' and six square items keyed to 'side × side'. The rectangle cases vary length and width independently rather than holding one of them fixed, for example 'a 2 by 5 rectangle takes 10 tiles', 'an 8 by 3 rectangle takes 24 tiles' and 'a 9 by 10 rectangle takes 90 tiles' in seed 601, so no narrower rule about a single dimension or a constant step fits the shown cases. Square items sweep sides of 2, 3, 4, 5 and 10 across the pool.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: Tile counts are supplied in the stem, so a grade 3 learner verifies a rule rather than computing area, and every product stays inside the tables through ten, the largest being 'a 10 by 10 square takes 100 tiles'. The rules are stated in words, 'side × side' and 'length × width', with no variable letters, no exponent notation, and no perimeter or unit-conversion vocabulary, so nothing from a later node is required to answer.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Thirteen of the fourteen samples carry distinct stems, spread across two figure types, two formatters, and two sentence frames: the main frame 'Cover each square with unit square tiles and count them' and the alternate 'Three squares are tiled with unit squares' closing with 'Which rule works for every one of them?'. Dimension sets differ item to item rather than repeating one triple. The one soft spot is that the alternate frame appears only on seeds 50 and 502, which render an identical stem, so it contributes just one distinct item and never lands on a rectangle; the pool is still varied enough that no answer can be pattern matched from the wording.

competency_alignment.rationale: The measuring unit is exactly the one the competency names, since every stem tiles with 'unit square tiles' and the quantity discussed is the tile count, which at this stage is the area in square units. Nothing outside the competency is smuggled in: no unit conversion, no missing-side solving, and no numeric area answer is demanded. What is asked for is the rule itself, 'length × width' or 'side × side', which is precisely the derivation the sentence calls for.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Side lengths run from 2 to 10 and tile counts from 'a 2 by 2 square takes 4 tiles' up to 'a 10 by 10 square takes 100 tiles', all inside grade 3 range and all small enough that a learner can believe the tiling was really carried out with tiles. Rectangle magnitudes match, topping out at 'a 9 by 10 rectangle takes 90 tiles', and every stated tile count in all 14 samples is arithmetically correct.
